author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: No One Is a Prize
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The visitor made the remark over a platter of roasted mushrooms.

He had come from a distant island, arrived through the Tideglass Door, and spent most of the afternoon telling anyone who would listen about a sea voyage I suspected grew longer each time he described it.

Maui knew him. That was the problem.

"Biggest fish I've ever seen," the visitor said, stretching both arms wide.

Maui grinned. "You've forgotten the one that nearly ate your boat."

"That was a different fish!"

They laughed. I laughed too. It was easy, for a while, to enjoy the sound of two people remembering a life that existed before I knew either of them.

Then the visitor turned toward me.

"And you must be his reward," he said.

I thought I'd misheard.

"Excuse me?"

"For all his heroic deeds! The gods finally sent him someone worth keeping. Maui always did know how to win a prize."

The platter stayed warm in my hands.

Around us, the Lanternwell feast continued. Mara was arguing with a customer about the price of honey. Tamsin had brought her repaired sixth table. Iroh was pouring tea, and Greg had taken his guitar out only long enough to tune it.

Maui laughed.

Not cruelly. Not even deliberately. It was an old reflex, the easy bark of somebody who had heard a hundred boasts and knew how to answer them.

It still hurt.

I put the platter down.

"I'm not a prize," I said.

The visitor blinked.

"Only a compliment."

"It isn't one."

He looked at Maui, as though Maui could explain why the property had started speaking.

"Come now, surely you know what I meant."

"I know what you said."

Maui stopped smiling.

For a moment I saw every muscle in his shoulders bunch. The hook on his back gleamed where the lamplight caught its curve. I knew the posture: the great Maui was about to make an example of someone.

Mini Maui planted his tiny feet against his chest and shook his head so violently that the tattooed hair bounced.

"What?" Maui whispered.

The miniature pointed to me instead of the visitor.

Maui exhaled through his nose. His grin came back, but it was sharp at the edges.

"Friend," he told the man, "I have fought things larger and uglier than that sentence. Don't make me waste a perfectly good feast on it."

I felt my own hands shake with anger. Maui saw that and took a step back, leaving me space to answer. He wasn't suddenly calm. He was furious enough to split a serving platter. He simply wasn't making my objection disappear inside his heroic rescue.

Later, when we had a moment alone, he admitted he had laughed because he'd liked being congratulated. He didn't try to dress the mistake up as a noble misunderstanding.

"The applause gets to me," he said. "Doesn't make it right."

The visitor waved a hand.

"Don't make a storm over a small phrase. You look happy together. That's all."

"Then you can say we look happy together."

The words came out steady. I was pleased about that, because my hands had begun to shake.

Maui opened his mouth.

I looked at him.

"Please don't smooth this over for him."

He closed it.

Silence reached our corner of the table, then broke around it as people resumed conversations. The visitor's expression hardened with embarrassment.

"I was teasing."

"I heard you."

"Your partner doesn't seem offended."

Maui put his cup down.

"My partner can speak for themself," he said.

I appreciated that, but I still wanted to ask him why he had laughed. Not here. Not while the visitor was looking for an audience. The question belonged between us.

The man took his drink and went to find another table.

I carried the mushrooms to the serving bench. Mara accepted the platter and gave me a look I couldn't quite read.

"Would you like to sit in the back for a minute?" she asked.

"No, thank you."

"Good. I was going to ask you to slice bread."

I almost smiled.

She handed me a knife. We worked together while the celebration moved around us, a small pocket of ordinary labor that didn't require me to explain how I felt.

After a while Maui came beside the table.

"Can I help?"

Mara pointed him toward the bread baskets.

"You can carry those to the other end without turning it into a victory march."

"I have never turned bread into a victory march."

"There's still time."

He obeyed.

We didn't speak privately until the last plates were collected and the lanterns began to dim. The visitor had already left. Nobody had chased him away, but nobody had offered a second audience either.

Maui found me at the well.

"You were angry," he said.

"Yes."

"With him?"

"Yes."

He paused.

"With me?"

I turned to him.

"Yes."

He flinched, just a little.

"I didn't mean to laugh at you."

"I know."

"He says things like that. Always has. We used to make it into a competition, who had the biggest tale or the best ending. I heard the joke before I heard the words."

"I could tell."

He looked miserable.

Part of me wanted to comfort him immediately. I cared about him. Seeing him upset still made me want to reach for his hand. But if I rescued every conversation before he'd understood the problem, neither of us would learn much.

"Tell me what you heard after I spoke," I said.

He leaned on the railing.

"That you aren't something I won. That nobody sent you as a reward. That you're here because you chose to be."

"Yes."

He looked toward the arches.

"And I shouldn't have laughed."

"You can laugh at an old joke and still realize it wasn't fair. I'm not asking you to become someone who never gets things wrong. I'm asking you to notice when the joke makes me smaller."

Maui nodded slowly.

"I thought if I fought him in front of everyone, it would turn into a performance."

"It might have."

"I thought staying quiet meant I was protecting you."

"Sometimes people need support. Sometimes they need space. You can ask."

He touched the bandage on his hand, now smaller than before.

"Like the rope."

"Like the rope."

There was a pause long enough for the square to settle into evening. Someone rang the last market bell. A cart rattled past the bakery, its wheels catching on the seam between stones.

"Do you want me to speak to him?" Maui asked.

"Not on my behalf. I said what I needed."

"And if he does it again?"

"Then we tell him he can't keep insulting people at our table. Together."

He considered that.

"You know," he said, "I once stole a whole island for somebody I thought I had to impress."

I looked at him.

"You did what?"

"Long story."

"I imagine the island found it long too."

He grinned, briefly. Then he grew serious.

"You make me think about what I call mine."

I touched his wrist.

"You can call me your partner. When I agree to it."

"I do."

"And I can call you mine in the same way."

"Please."

I stepped closer. His hand found the small of my back, not possessive, simply steady. He waited as I tilted my face toward him.

"You don't have to earn me with a legend," I said.

"I know."

"Do you?"

"I'm trying."

I kissed him. The first touch was almost shy. He answered with a warmth that made my knees briefly forget their job. When we drew apart, I rested my forehead against his, and we laughed softly at the absurdity of two people who could argue about language and still become hopelessly distracted by each other.

At home, we ate the last of Mara's bread and talked about the first time we'd each been treated as somebody else's story.

Maui told me about people praising his strength without ever learning what frightened him. I told him how much I hated the assumption that my missing memories made me easy to define.

He listened without trying to fix it.

The candles burned low. He brushed his thumb along my palm and asked whether I wanted him to stay.

"Yes," I said.

The kitchen grew quiet. We closed the door and left the rest of the evening to ourselves.

In the morning, a small note had appeared beneath the lantern hooks.

The visitor had left an apology, awkwardly phrased, with no request that I accept it. Maui showed it to me but did not tell me what to feel.

I folded it and placed it in my notebook.

At the next feast, I would speak my own name.

That should never have needed to be a victory.

It still felt like one.
